summary: Specifies DHCPv6 options, called Softwire46 options, to configure Customer Edge devices that use address-plus-port schemes for IPv4 over IPv6. The options carry the parameters for those schemes.

eli5.summary: A starter packet that tells your home router which settings to use to talk to the old internet.

questions: how does a map-e ce get its configuration
subtitle: How a DHCPv6 server hands a home router the settings it needs to carry IPv4 over an IPv6-only network.

tldr.problem: A Customer Edge (CE) router on an IPv6-only access network needs its IPv4 address or shared address, port ranges, and the mode (tunnel or translation) before it can offer IPv4 service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines eight DHCPv6 options, called Softwire46 options: five building-block options and three container options, one for each of MAP-E, MAP-T and Lightweight 4over6. The client asks for a container in its Option Request Option, and the server fills it with the right building blocks.
tldr.outcome: Provisioning is tied to the lifetime of the customer's IPv6 prefix. RFC 7598 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8539.

today: RFC 7598 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8539. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Softwire46 Needs DHCPv6 Options
sections.content:
Several designs from the IETF Softwire Working Group give users IPv4 over a service provider's IPv6 network using Address plus Port (A+P). A CE router in such a domain needs to know its IPv4 address and its transport-layer port range or ranges. It also needs to know whether the IPv6 transport mode is encapsulation or translation.

This RFC specifies DHCPv6 options to deliver those parameters to CE routers. Other IPv4 configuration that is not derived from the A+P parameters is not covered; the RFC expects that to keep using DHCPv4. Configuring the Border Relay (BR) is out of scope.
sections.eli5: A router that wants to use the old internet over the new one needs an address and a set of allowed doors. This RFC says how to hand those over.

sections.title: Three Mechanisms, One Option Family
sections.content:
The options configure three mechanisms: MAP-E (RFC 7597), MAP-T (RFC 7599) and Lightweight 4over6 (RFC 7596). They provide the same functionality, IPv4 service to a CE over an IPv6-only access network. MAP-E uses IPv4-over-IPv6 tunneling, MAP-T uses IPv4-to-IPv6 translation, and Lightweight 4over6 is a hub-and-spoke tunneling mechanism with zero embedded address bits.

Each mechanism has its own container option. A client asks for a mechanism by putting that container's option code in its DHCPv6 Option Request Option (ORO). The provisioning parameters then arrive as common options embedded inside the container. Clients that receive provisioning options outside a container MUST silently ignore them.

The provisioning is tied to the lifetime of the End-user IPv6 prefix, along with the validity of the address, port set, and any authorization and accounting.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to do the job, and each has its own envelope. You ask for the envelope you want, and the settings come inside it.

sections.title: The Common Options
sections.content:
Five options carry the parameters. OPTION_S46_RULE conveys the Basic Mapping Rule (BMR) and optionally a Forwarding Mapping Rule (FMR); it holds a flags byte, ea-len (0 to 48), prefix4-len (0 to 32), an IPv4 prefix, prefix6-len (0 to 128) and an IPv6 prefix. If the F-flag is set, the rule is used as an FMR; if not, it is a BMR only and MUST NOT be used for forwarding.

OPTION_S46_BR carries one 16-octet IPv6 address of the Border Relay. Redundancy can be done with an anycast address, and several BR options MAY be included.

OPTION_S46_DMR carries the Default Mapping Rule as an IPv6 prefix, from which MAP-T builds IPv6 destination addresses by embedding an IPv4 address. OPTION_S46_V4V6BIND carries the full or shared IPv4 address of a Lightweight 4over6 CE, plus the IPv6 prefix the CE uses as the tunnel source.

All of them use addresses, not FQDNs.
sections.eli5: Inside the envelopes are small cards: one with the rules for working out your address, one with the address of the gateway, one with the default route, and one with your address on the old internet.

sections.title: Port Parameters
sections.content:
With address sharing, many CEs use the same IPv4 address and each gets its own set of ports. OPTION_S46_PORTPARAMS is optional and describes that set. It has an offset (0 to 15), a PSID-len (the number of significant bits, also called k) and a 16-bit PSID. The address-sharing ratio is 2^k. If PSID-len is 0, the PSID field is ignored.

When a client receives this option with an explicit PSID, it MUST use that PSID when configuring its softwire interface. The option MUST be discarded if the CE is not configured with a full IPv4 address (for example, an IPv4 prefix). It is contained in an OPTION_S46_RULE or an OPTION_S46_V4V6BIND option. The MAP algorithm itself is described in RFC 7597.
sections.eli5: If many houses share one address, each house gets its own set of doors. This option says which doors are yours.

sections.title: Containers and Encapsulation Rules
sections.content:
The three containers are OPTION_S46_CONT_MAPE (94), OPTION_S46_CONT_MAPT (95) and OPTION_S46_CONT_LW (96). Each holds encapsulated options, and a DHCPv6 message MAY include several MAP-E containers to represent multiple domains.

Which options are mandatory, optional or not permitted depends on the container. A MAP-E container needs at least one rule option and at least one BR option. A MAP-T container needs at least one rule option and exactly one DMR option. A Lightweight 4over6 container needs at most one binding option and at least one BR option. Clients that receive a container that violates these rules MUST silently ignore it.
sections.eli5: Each envelope has a list of cards it must contain, may contain, or must not contain. If an envelope breaks its list, you throw it away.

sections.title: Server and Client Behavior
sections.content:
By default, a server will not send a Softwire46 container unless the client listed it in its ORO. If the client lists several, the server replies with the containers for which it has configuration. A client MUST request the containers it is configured for in SOLICIT, REQUEST, RENEW, REBIND and INFORMATION-REQUEST messages.

Clients can send options with values as hints; the server may accept or ignore them, and clients MUST be able to process values that differ from their hints. A client MUST support multiple rule options in a MAP-E or MAP-T container. A client that gets an unsupported option or invalid value SHOULD discard that container and log the event. A CE with several interfaces handles each interface separately.

Choosing between several mechanisms and failure handling are out of scope.
sections.eli5: The router has to ask for the envelope by name, or it will not get one. If an envelope looks wrong, it puts it aside and writes a note.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As with all DHCPv6 configuration, the settings could come from a third party in the middle, so there is no basis on which access over MAP or Lightweight 4over6 can be trusted. Softwires therefore should not bypass security mechanisms such as IP firewalls.

In IPv6-only networks that lack IPv4 firewalls, a device that supports MAP could be tricked into enabling its IPv4 stack and sending IPv4 traffic to an attacker. The RFC points readers to the security sections of RFC 7597, RFC 7596 and RFC 7599, and to Secure DHCPv6, a Work in Progress at the time.
sections.eli5: Someone could slip your router a fake settings sheet. So keep your own locks on the doors even when the sheet looks right.

fields.name: option-length
fields.desc: Length of the option after these two fields.

fields.name: offset
fields.desc: PSID offset; allowed values are 0 to 15.

fields.name: PSID-len
fields.desc: Number of significant bits in the PSID (k).

fields.name: PSID
fields.desc: Port Set Identifier; first k bits hold the value, the rest are zero padding.
